-=== Asynchronous Data Management
-
-Any dropping of asynchronous data must happen at the source, to ensure that the data loss is recoverable.  An AMB implementation must apply backpressure to the source to avoid scenarios where asynchronous data may be dropped downstream from the source.

-====
-_Asynchronous data loss typically results from scenarios where the data is being produced faster than the AMB can consume it.  If this persists, any internal buffering will fill and new data will have to be dropped.  Once internal buffers are able to drain, new data can again be consumed.  The data source is expected to ensure that processing software can recover from any data loss, which may require indication of the data loss within the data stream._
-

+=== Asynchronous Write Privilege and Address Translation
 
 The effective privilege mode of AMB writes is selected by bits associated with each AMB instance in `menvcfg` and, if the H extension is implemented, `henvcfg`.  For the AMB associated with self-hosted trace (STRC), the full set of configuration options is illustrated below.

 |===
-| `menvcfg`.STRCS | `henvcfg`.STRCV | Privilege | Translation
+| `menvcfg`.STRCS | `henvcfg`.STRCV | Effective Privilege Mode | Translation
 | 0 | - | M-mode | None (Bare)
 | 1 | 0 | S/HS-mode | `satp`
 | 1 | 1 | VS-mode | `vsatp`/`hgatp`
 |===

-====
-_Using a fixed effective privilege mode for asynchronous data writes, rather than using the current privilege mode, allows supporting system-wide uses, where recording persists across privilege modes._
-
-_This mechanism is also motivated by an expectation that implementations may buffer asynchronous data internally before it is emitted to the AMB, in order to avoid data loss during asynchronous data bursts.  This translation approach avoids the need to delay traps and trap returns by requiring internal buffers to be flushed before the current privilege mode changes.  Asynchronous data can continue to be emitted with the same privilege and translation despite changes to the current privilege mode._

+[[ambtlb]]
+==== Caching AMB Address Translations
 
-_Cached AMB page translations can be flushed by SFENCE and HFENCE instructions, globally or per ASID/VMID, just as other translations are.  Such fence operations may result in asynchronous data loss if performed while AMB is enabled and not empty._
-====
+Implementations should cache AMB address translations in order to improve performance and avoid asynchronous data loss.  Cached AMB page translations can be flushed by SFENCE and HFENCE instructions, globally or per ASID/VMID, just as other translations are.  See <<sfence.vma>> and <<hfence.vma>>.  
+
+NOTE: _Depending on the AMB size and the asynchronous data rate, AMB writes can touch many pages in a short amount of time.  However, AMB uses page translations efficiently, writing exclusively to a single page until it is full, then moving to the next and writing exclusively to it.  Rather than allowing AMB writes to displace explicit memory access translations from the primary TLB, it may be more efficient to store cached AMB translations in a very small dedicated AMB TLB.  Two entries (current page and next page) will be sufficient for most implementations, though more may be warranted if the implementation pre-translates more than one page ahead._
+
+To avoid asynchronous data loss, software must disable AMB (as prescribed in <<ambendis>>) before invalidating an active AMB TLB entry.  Active AMB TLB entries include the current AMB page (that is, the page that holds the address in `sambaddr`) and the pre-translated page(s) immediately following, which may be written in the event the data source is disabled and flushed.  An AMB page can only be pre-translated and translation-cached if it is present and writable by the AMB's effective privilege mode.
+
+If the current AMB page translation is invalidated, AMB will backpressure the source until the translation cache entry is restored.  If internal buffers fill in the interim, the source may have to drop data.  Further, if any pre-translated and active AMB TLB entries are invalidated, internally buffered data may not be able to be flushed without a trap, which risks unrecoverable data loss.  See <<ambpretrans>> for details.
+
+Any AMB and corresponding data source that software disabled in order to invalidate a TLB entry can be re-enabled afterward, using the guidance in <<ambendis>>.
+
+[[ambpretrans]]
+==== AMB Page Pre-translation
+
+Any loss of asynchronous data is undesirable, but it is at times unavoidable.  Asynchronous data loss falls into two categories:
+
+** *Recoverable data loss*, which occurs when data is dropped by the data source.  The source can ensure that data is dropped on record (or packet/message) boundaries, and that software is provided with any information needed to process the data despite the loss.
+** *Unrecoverable data loss*, which occurs when data is dropped downstream from the source.  In this case data loss may not be aligned with data record boundaries, and hence partial records may be observed.  Software is typically not able to process impacted records and, depending on the encoding scheme, may not be able to process any data following the loss.
+
+Implementations should endeavor to minimize recoverable data loss, while unrecoverable data loss must be avoided entirely for software that follows the guidance provided in this specification.  To accomplish the latter, implementations must follow the guidelines below.
+
+. While AMB is enabled (`sambcs`.EN=1), utilize AMB page pre-translation to ensure that all data residing in internal buffers can be flushed without requiring a trap (translation fault or guest-page fault).
+** Pre-translation involves retrieving and caching address translations for not only the current AMB page (that is, the page that holds the AMB write pointer in `sambaddr`), but one or more following AMB pages.  A simple implementation would cache translations for the current and next AMB page.  When page X is filled, writes transition to (already translated) page X+1, and translation begins for page X+2.  The number of pages to pre-translate should be one more than is needed to flush all internally buffered data.
+** Flushes may be initiated in contexts where a trap cannot be properly handled; consider a translation fault raised while a hypervisor is saving guest AMB state during guest context switch.  In such cases, if AMB is disabled before internal buffers are fully flushed (i.e., `sambcs`.EN cleared while `sambcs`.EMPTY=0), data residing in internal buffers may be dropped in an unrecoverable manner.  Pre-translation avoids this by ensuring that a trap during flush is never necessary.
+** Pre-translation must be suspended when it encounters a translation fault or guest-page fault condition.  This ensures that the translation fault pointer (`sambcs`.TFPTR) is not overwritten by another translation fault for a programmatically younger page.  When suspended, pre-translation should resume when either `sambcs`.TF is cleared (translation fault serviced) or when the HFENCE.GVMA instruction completes (part of the guest-page fault handler flow).
+
+. Backpressure to the data source before the available space in translated AMB pages is less than the size of internal buffering.
+** Consider an implementation with 256 bytes of internal storage, and that pre-translates 1 page ahead.  If that pre-translation is delayed and `sambaddr` increments to within 256 bytes of the current page boundary, there is risk that a flush will require a trap.  By preemptively backpressuring to the source before this occurs, it is guaranteed that any data loss that could result is recoverable.
+
+. A guest-page fault condition encountered during pre-translation must be held pending while V=0.
+** This ensures that the exception is not taken when it could be destructive (e.g., when already executing a guest-page fault handler).
+** If AMB is disabled while such a guest-page fault is pending, the pending fault can be dropped.  The condition will be re-discovered if/when AMB is re-enabled with the same configuration.
+** If AMB writes are configured with VS-mode privilege, it is expected that the data source will be configured to inhibit asynchronous data generation when V=0.  However, buffered data may still be emitted while V=0.  The guidelines above ensure that no trap is required to complete a buffer flush, hence deferring the guest-page fault in such cases does not risk data loss.
+
+[[lambi-handling]]
+[appendix]
+=== Handling Local Asynchronous Memory Buffer Interrupts
+
+Local asynchronous memory buffer interrupts (LAMBIs) are raised as a result of either of the two conditions below.
+
+a. The buffer management mechanism is enabled (`sambcs`.BMIEN=1) and the buffer threshold has been reached (see `sambcs`.BMITH definition in <<sambcs>>).  In this case `sambcs`.BMI is set to 1.
+b. A translation fault was encountered while translating an AMB page.  In this case `sambcs`.TF is set to 1.
+
+Software should follow the sequence below when servicing a LAMBI in privilege mode _x_.
+
+For each `sambcs` register implemented:
+
+1. Disable the asynchronous data source following the guidance in <<ambendis>>.
+** This ensures that asychronous data generation ceases, and that all data generated has been emitted to the AMB.  This serves to avoid race conditions where conditions (a) and/or (b) above occur during LAMBI handler execution, which could result in the LAMBI being cleared without all causes being serviced.
+2. Clear `__x__ip`.LAMBI
+** Doing this after step 1 ensures that any LAMBI conditions that arise during step 1 do not result in a spurious LAMBI following this one.
+** This step must be done before step 4, but could optionally follow step 3.
+3. Service the LAMBI cause(s).
+** If `sambcs`.TF=1, call the appropriate routine to service the translation fault, then clear TF.  This routine may be shared with the page fault exception handler.
+** If `sambcs`.BMI=1, perform any buffer management tasks desired, including any modifications to the AMB configuration.  When collecting asynchronous data in age order, account for buffer wrap as recommended below.  Then clear BMI.
+*** If `sambcs`.WRAP=1, software should begin collection at the address held in `sambaddr`, which holds the programmatically oldest data.  Collection should wrap at buffer end to offset 0, then continue to `sambaddr`-1, which holds the programmatically youngest data.
+*** If `sambcs`.WRAP=0, software should begin collection at the base of the AMB (offset 0), which holds the programmatically oldest data.  Collection should continue to `sambaddr`-1, which holds the programmatically youngest data.
+4. Re-enable any data sources disabled in step 1, following the guidance in <<ambendis>>.
+** After this step asynchronous data generation resumes, which could result in a new LAMBI being pended.  Because `__x__status`.__x__IE=0 during handler execution, any new LAMBI will remain pending until the handler completes.
+** The handler could opt to perform step 4 for each AMB instance after steps 1-3 are completed for all instances, if data generation during handler execution is not desired.

 == Self-hosted Trace ISA Extension (Smstrce1p0/Ssstrce1p0 and Smstrcn1p0/Ssstrcn1p0)
 
+Self-hosted trace describes the use of hardware trace capabilities by software running on the target.  The Smstrc* extensions provide an ISA interface to the RISC-V trace encoder.  'Sm' and 'Ss' imply M-mode and S-mode extensions, respectively, while 'strc' refers to self-hosted trace.  The following 'e' vs 'n' selects the encoding standard; 'e' implies the standard defined in the Efficient Trace for RISC-V v2.0 specification, while 'n' implies the standard defined in the RISC-V N-trace v1.0 specification.  Finally, '1p0' implies self-hosted trace version 1.0 for each encoding scheme.
+
+Smstrc*/Ssstrc* utilize an asynchronous memory buffer (AMB) as the trace sink.  AMB is defined by the Ssamb extension, upon which Smstrc*/Ssstrc* depend.
+
+The machine-level extensions, Smstrc*, encompasses all newly added Control Status Registers (CSRs), instructions, and behavior modifications for a hart across all privilege levels. The corresponding supervisor-level extensions, Ssstrc*, are essentially identical to the corresponding Smstrc* extension, except that it excludes machine-level CSRs and behaviors not intended to be directly accessible at the supervisor level.
+

+[appendix]
+=== Configuration Scenarios
+
+This section describes likely self-hosted trace configurations for select scenarios in a typical "rich OS" environment.  Note that this list is far from comprehensive, and there are scenarios where many more combinations of the bits below may be appropriate.
+
+.Self-hosted Trace Configuration Scenarios
+[options="header"]
+|===
+| Tracing | Application | OS | Application(s) + OS | Guest | Guest (emulated) | Guest(s) + Hypervisor
+| `mstateen0`.STRC | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1
+| `hstateen0`.STRC | NA | NA | NA | 1 | 0 | 0
+| `menvcfg`.STRCS | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1
+| `menvcfg`.STRCV | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0
+| `mideleg`.LAMBI | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1
+| `hideleg`.LAMBI | NA | NA | NA | 1 | 1 | 0
+| `mstrcctl`.M | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0
+| `mstrcctl`.S | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1
+| `mstrcctl`.U | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1
+| `vsstrcctl`.S | NA | NA | NA | 1 | 1 | 1
+| `vsstrcctl`.U | NA | NA | NA | 1 | 1 | 1
+|===
+
+The "Application", "OS", and "Application(s) + OS" scenarios assume a bare-metal (V=0) configuration where only a user-mode application, the operating system, or some combination of the two, respectively, are traced.  The remaining scenarios assume a virtualized environment.  The "Guest" column assumes that a virtualization guest is accessing self-hosted trace directly.  The "Guest (emulated)" column assumes that the hypervisor is emulating guest access to self-hosted trace state, either via trap-and-emulate or via hypercall.  And finally, the "Guest(s) + Hypervisor" column assumes a hypervisor that is tracing both itself and one or more guests.
+
+All selected scenarios involve delegation of self-hosted trace (`mstateen0`.STRC) and LAMBI interrupts (`mideleg`.LAMBI) to S-mode, to allow the kernel/hypervisor control of the capability.  Only in scenarios where a guest is accessing self-hosted trace state directly is self-hosted trace further delegated to VS-mode (`hstateen0`.STRC).  And only in scenarios where the effective privilege mode of trace writes is VS-mode are LAMBIs further delegated to VS-mode (`hideleg`.LAMBI), to allow the guest to service VS-stage translation faults and buffer management interrupts.
+
+When tracing only while V=0, S-mode is chosen as the effective privilege mode of trace writes (`menvcfg`.STRCS and `henvcfg`.STRCV).  This allows the AMB to reside in kernel address space.  See <<ambaddr>> for configuration details.  When a virtualization guest is tracing ("Guest" column), or a hypervisor is emulating self-hosted trace on behalf of a guest ("Guest (emulated)" column) but allowing the guest to manage the AMB, VS-mode is chosen as the effective privilege mode of trace writes.  This allows the AMB to reside in guest address space.  And finally, when a hypervisor is tracing itself + guest(s) ("Guest(s) + Hypervisor" column), S-mode is chosen as the effective privilege mode of trace writes, allowing the AMB to reside in hypervisor address space.
+
+NOTE: _A hypervisor might prefer a different configuration for the "Guest (emulated)" scenario.  One alternative would be for the AMB to be managed entirely by the hypervisor, and hence reside in hypervisor address space.  Such a configuration would choose S-mode as the effective privilege mode for trace writes, and would not further delegate LAMBIs to VS-mode._
+
+The privilege mode filtering configurations chosen above simply reflect the modes in which each scenario chooses to trace.  There are many other configuration options within self-hosted trace, but they are orthogonal to these scenarios.
